The how-to's stated reason to prefer it — the corpus-wide record "carries the raw `:exception`" (`API.md:585`, `009:1235`, how-to `:275`) — is not a discriminator: the sink delivers `:exception` too under its default profile. `projection.cljc:352-360` drops it only under `:rf.egress/public-error`, and the how-to says so itself at `:305` ("leaving the profile off keeps the exception"). What the raw door genuinely carries that the sink does not is (i) FRAMELESS records and (ii) declaring once per process — `:observability` is accepted on `make-frame`/`frame-root` only; `configure!` (`core.cljc:2620`) has no such key.
- **AI agent.** Two spellings for one job, the spec and the teaching corpus in disagreement, and a how-to sentence ("That's the whole surface for now", `:35`) that is false about the surface the spec calls normal. `spec/Principles.md` §Regularity over cleverness: "there is one obvious way to do a thing."
- **Tool author.** Registering ANY `:errors` listener silences the dev console for every frame, "even if that listener ignores this category" (`error_emit.cljc:121-132`); Story registers a no-op to claim the stream (`shell.cljs:1153`). rf2-kuky.18 (in progress, PR #9306) is keying the console on nothing-routed-this-record so Story owns errors as frame policy instead. Once that lands, the raw door's last tool-tier use is hicasso's one-render window.

### The hard constraint: frameless records — verified at tip

Three producers emit records with `:frame nil`, and today those records reach ONLY the corpus-wide stream:

1. `:rf.error/no-frame-context` — `frame.cljc:804-952` (`no-frame-context-payload` at `:834`, `emit-no-frame-context!` at `:906`); by construction there is no frame to stamp.
2. The pre-frame SSR hydration-parse arm of `:rf.error/malformed-hydration-payload` — `error_emit.cljc:815-830` documents the union shape's `:frame <id-or-nil>` "(the pre-frame hydration-parse FRAMELESS case …)"; the late-bind directory entry `:error-emit/dispatch-error-record` (`directory.cljc:902`) names it explicitly.
3. hicasso's `compute-sub` errors — `server.cljs:221-222`: "`:rf.error/sub-exception` is stamped `:frame nil` BY CONSTRUCTION — a pure fn has no frame in scope to stamp". Its `watch-recovered-errors!` (`:254-295`) registers on `:errors` for exactly this reason, "measured rather than stylistic" — the per-frame SSR buffer read CLEAN on the failure it exists to catch.

The sink route refuses them by design: `route-error-record!` is "a NO-OP when the record's `:frame` is unresolved … incl. the FRAMELESS `:frame nil` records, which carry no frame-owned sink policy by definition" (`observability.cljc:317-322`; `frame-observability` at `:150-157` returns nil on a nil id; `error_emit.cljc:909` repeats it at the call site). So **retiring the stream before the process default exists opens a gap: those three categories reach nobody.** A1 (the default) must land before A2 (the retirement), and the ordering is structural, not a preference.

A second dependency underneath: "project under no frame" is not expressible today. `elision.cljc:1128` resolves the governing frame as `(or (:frame opts) (rf.frame/resolve-current-frame))`, so an explicit nil falls through to the AMBIENT frame; `projection.cljc:572-575` seeds `:frame` from the record by truthiness the same way. rf2-kuky.5 (open, dispatchable) makes explicit nil fail closed. A1 is blocked on it.

### The strongest counter-evidence

Codex holds the opposite position and said so without hedging. From the epic (rf2-kuky notes, "One-reviewer findings"): "this corpus only; **codex explicitly did not verify them and calls them larger design decisions** … Codex's caution on these is worth carrying: one documented home per operation supports the accepted cleanups, but does not by itself justify removing every facade export or building a universal clear/query/configure language." From the observability doc itself: "Retiring public `:errors`/`:events` listeners and adding process-wide policy inheritance is a larger redesign than the evidence presently earns. Raw synchronous capture and projected delivery are different operations, even if both ultimately register callbacks in maps. Two empty application consumer lists do not establish equivalence." And: "Do not add a process default merely to make deletion of an existing door possible. If a real multi-frame integration later needs it, specify absent policy versus explicit empty policy, per-stream inheritance versus whole-map replacement, frameless records, teardown records whose owner no longer resolves, and prevention of duplicate delivery. These are semantic choices, not simply one fallback branch."

The tree gives Codex two real facts. hicasso's `capture-intents` (`test.cljs:567-603`) is a shipped test-kit port built on the corpus-wide `:events` record and filtered by `:frame` — a synchronous raw capture, not a projected egress. And hicasso `server.cljs:254-295` chose the raw stream after measuring the projected route failing on frameless records. Both survive under A — through `re-frame.event-emit` / `re-frame.error-emit` directly, implementation tier — but "moved out of sight" is exactly Codex's objection. Note also that `spec/Principles.md` §Regularity permits "the documented alternative with a stated use case"; A's answer is that the stated use case (raw exception) is false and the true ones (frameless, declare-once) are what A1 absorbs.

Grok took the middle: A, but in two beads, and "Zero in-repo app consumers of either door means we do not yet know how a Sentry bridge will actually be written. Deleting the advanced door before the replacement exists is the one way this can fail closed on frameless records."

## The decision

**Which door(s) does the library offer an application for production observation of errors and events?**

- **A.** One door. Frame `:observability` + a `configure! {:observability …}` process default, wired by `register-observability-sink!`. `register-listener!` keeps `#{:trace :epoch}`. Two implementation beads, A1 then A2.
- **B.** Two doors, as designed. `:events`/`:errors` stay public as the documented advanced corpus-wide hook; no process default; rf2-kuky.21's §8 "Advanced" section becomes the permanent home, with the one discriminator sentence.
- **C.** The process default now (A1 alone); retirement revisited once a real Sentry bridge exists in the corpus.

Under A or C the ruling also settles seven routing questions. Recommended answers, for Mike to accept "as recommended" or amend:

| # | Question | Recommended |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Precedence | per STREAM: a frame that declares a stream (even `[]`) uses its own entries; a frame that omits it inherits the default's entries for that stream. Whole-map replacement rejected (forces every frame with one custom sink to restate the default). |
| 2 | Absent vs explicit empty | as 1; `[]` is the opt-out; `{:observability nil}` on `configure!` clears the default. Validation reuses `frame_classification.cljc`'s validator at call time, fail-loud, reusing `:rf.error/bad-frame-classification` with `:where 'rf/configure!` — no new category. Not an `assert` (rf2-xn13's rule; the existing guard at `core.cljc:2668-2683` is the model). |
| 3 | Frameless records | process default only; projected with `{:frame nil}` → fail-closed per `015:251` case 3. Blocked on rf2-kuky.5. |
| 4 | Records whose `:frame` no longer resolves (destroyed / dissociated incarnation) | route to the process default under fail-closed projection. `015:296` forbids borrowing ANOTHER FRAME's policy; the process default is not a frame's. `capture_frame_reincarnation_sink_route_cljs_test.cljc` pins only that a dissociated id must not resolve to a same-id successor — compatible. **This is the one answer with no precedent in the tree; it needs Mike's actual choice.** |
| 5 | Duplicate delivery | exactly one policy source per record; a sink id present in both frame and default is invoked once. |
| 6 | Raw cross-frame hook | an explicit `:rf.egress/local-raw` entry on the process default (enum member verified). |
| 7 | Console fallback | composes with rf2-kuky.18: a process-default delivery to a registered sink owns the record. |

## Options

### A. One door — process default first, retirement second (fable, Grok; recommended)
DOSSIER ATTACHMENT (continued, piece 2/3, verbatim, contiguous with the previous piece):
**What changes.** A1: `configure!` gains `:observability` (`core.cljc:2620`, delegating to a `re-frame.observability/configure!` over a `defonce` default atom); `frame-observability` resolves per stream against the default; `route-error!` / `route-error-record!` / `route-handled-event!` gain the frameless and unresolved-owner arms; one conformance fixture beside `spec/conformance/fixtures/data-classification-observability-sink-receives-projected-record.edn`. A2: `listener-streams` → `#{:trace :epoch}`; the `:events`/`:errors` `case` arms, docstring and `unknown-listener-stream!` message; four consumers migrate (hicasso `server.cljs:287` → `re-frame.error-emit`, `test.cljs:597,603` → `re-frame.event-emit`, `elision_demo.cljs:243,249` → a `:handled-events` sink on its frame, Story `shell.cljs:1153` already gone under .18); `frame.cljc:2810,3948` and `ssr.cljc:388` are already on the implementation registry and do not move. A3: one note on rf2-xpd8 (closed 2026-09-05) that "listener" in its ruling now names `re-frame.error-emit/register-error-listener!`.

**What it costs.** Breadth, not depth. Tests: 66 files on the `:errors` facade + 16 on `:events` at tip (bead said 61 + 16) migrate to the implementation namespaces or — better — to a `re-frame.test-support` capture bracket, the sibling of rf2-64iuw's trace-recorder bracket. Teaching: 16 files (docs 4, spec 2, skills 9, migration README 1 — list in the bead). Hot zone, sequential: `spec/API.md` (§Event-emit/§Error-emit `:571-591` fold into §Frame-owned sinks `:699`, §Observation listeners `:593-606`, §Configure keys `:895`), `spec/009` (`:643`, `:1124`, `:1214-1284`, `:1285`, `:2689`), `spec/Spec-Schemas.md:4341-4350`, `spec/002-Frames.md:647-659`, `spec/Conventions.md:1327-1331`, `spec/Tool-Pair.md` attach table, `migration/from-re-frame-v1/README.md` M-13 rows, `api-manifest-metadata.edn` then regenerate. A new `configure` key is a Spec change by the fixed-and-additive rule (`API.md` §Fixed-and-additive) — fine, additive. Removing two members of a closed stream vocabulary is a Spec-ulation "breakage"; the posture answers it (pre-alpha, a redundant spelling is deleted). Risk: fail-open ONLY if A2 lands before A1 — which the bead ordering forbids — and frameless projection is only as safe as rf2-kuky.5. Behaviour change for a library that wanted a cross-frame hook without touching frame config: it now calls `configure!` once.

**What it buys.** The surface says what the spec says. `register-listener!` means one thing (raw dev stream, both members DCE'd); `register-observability-sink!` means one thing (projected production egress). A multi-frame app declares once. Frameless records get a projected home for the first time (today they have only the raw one). The fail-open door leaves the first-search path.

### B. Two doors, as designed — the raw stream stays the documented advanced hook (Codex)

**What changes.** Nothing beyond rf2-kuky.17–.21. The how-to's §8 "Advanced — the corpus-wide listener" (as .21 rewrites it) is the permanent home; `spec/API.md:585` and `spec/009:1235` gain .21's one sentence: the sink also delivers `:exception` under the default profile; what the corpus-wide stream alone carries is a frameless record and a declaration made once per process.

**What it costs.** Two production doors persist for one job, with the fail-open one still one search away and still the simpler-looking one (one call, no frame config). `register-listener!` keeps mixing DCE'd and always-on streams. A multi-frame app declares a policy on every frame. Frameless records stay raw-only. The rf2-xpd8 vocabulary needs nothing. Zero migration.

**What it buys.** Zero churn against ~82 test files and 16 teaching files. Keeps hicasso's measured one-render window on the public verb, and keeps `capture-intents` on the public `:events` port. Matches Codex: "Trusting programmers supports an explicitly advanced raw hook beside the normal projected path." Honest reading of Principles §Regularity, which allows a documented alternative with a stated use case — once .21 states the true one.

### C. Process default now, retirement later (Grok's "third, cheaper path")

**What changes.** A1 only: `configure! {:observability …}`, frameless routing, unresolved-owner routing, the conformance fixture. `:events`/`:errors` stay public.

**What it costs.** All of A1's semantic work (questions 1–7) for a knob with zero consumers today, while the interval has THREE ways to declare production observation (frame policy, process default, raw stream) — the count goes up before it comes down, and "later" has no trigger unless the ruling names one (recommended un-park trigger: the first real bridge in `examples/` or a consumer app, per Principles §The demand bar's "pre-settled promotion shape"). Blocked on rf2-kuky.5 exactly as A1 is.

**What it buys.** The cheapest reversible position. The frameless home is built before anything is deleted, so nothing can fail closed on those records; a real bridge can be written on the sink + default and observed before the raw door goes. If it is never missed, A2 files itself.

## Recommendation

**A, as two beads in order — and the fallback is C, which is A1 alone.** The spec already ruled which door is normal (`API.md:585`, `009:1235`, `015:270`), and a surface that contradicts its own spec's ruling is the thing this wave exists to fix; Principles §Regularity over cleverness wants "one obvious way", and the one stated use case that licensed the alternative (raw exception) is false at tip (`projection.cljc:352-360`). The two true carries — frameless records and declare-once — are precisely what A1 delivers, and A1 gives frameless records a PROJECTED home they have never had, closing a fail-open posture the spec never names (a public verb that bypasses the projector entirely; Principles §Low hidden context). After A2, both members of `register-listener!` are DCE'd and both members of the production door are projected: the vocabulary carries the tier. The masterpiece posture is the tiebreaker against Codex's "larger redesign than the evidence earns": the cost is mechanical breadth in tests, the depth is one atom and one fallback branch, and pre-alpha is when a redundant public door is deleted rather than documented. The implementation registries Codex wants preserved ARE preserved, just not as public spellings — which is the same one-home-per-operation rule Codex endorsed for the accepted cleanups. Precedent for a process default with per-frame override already lives inside `configure!`: `:trace-buffer {:events-retained N}` applies "to `:rf/default` and to every frame that did not set its own `:rf.trace/events-retained` metadata" (`core.cljc:2622-2631`).

**If Mike disagrees:** C is the right hedge, not B — B leaves frameless records raw-only and the count at two; C builds the home, keeps the door, and lets a real bridge decide. Choose B only if Mike wants the raw synchronous-capture door to be a permanent PUBLIC contract for tools like hicasso's test-kit, rather than an implementation seam.

**Filed / dispatched on each outcome.**
- **A:** file A1 (`blocks:` rf2-kuky.5 and rf2-kuky.17; rf2-xn13 is CLOSED at tip so the bead's third blocker has lapsed — the guard is already always-on at `core.cljc:2668-2683`), carrying the seven answers verbatim; file A2 blocked on A1, rf2-kuky.18, .19, .21, with consumer counts re-measured at filing; post A3 as a note on rf2-xpd8 (closed; a note is fine). Hot-zone sequencing: A1 and A2 each touch `spec/API.md`, `spec/002`, `spec/Spec-Schemas.md`; neither may run beside .17, .20 or .21 on the same file.
- **B:** close rf2-kuky.22 with the reason; name rf2-kuky.21's §8 the permanent home; nothing else files.
- **C:** file A1 only, with the un-park trigger for A2 written into A1's description.

## Codex Recommendation

### Choose B: retain independent observation; make projected delivery the obvious default

The teaching problem is real, but these are not equivalent operations. Keep `:events` and `:errors` on the public listener verb; lead ordinary production integration with frame-owned projected sinks. Do not add process-wide inheritance solely to remove two stream keywords. This recommendation follows a fresh source review, not the earlier Codex position quoted above.

The strongest case for A is good: configure monitoring once, cover frameless failures, and avoid teaching every integration to reconstruct projection. That could earn a process default independently. However, A's proposed fallback does **not** replace the existing cross-frame observation contract, and the implementation is deeper than an atom plus a fallback branch. Pre-alpha permits breaking changes; it does not make different operations redundant.

### Three distinctions the decision must retain

**1. A default is not an independent observer.** Under the proposed per-stream precedence, `{:errors []}` or a frame's custom error entries prevent the process default from receiving that frame's errors. Consequently a process-default `:rf.egress/local-raw` entry is not a replacement for a listener that watches every emission regardless of that frame's monitoring configuration. This is a direct consequence of A's routing rules, not a hypothetical implementation bug. Independent listeners also compose by id without integrations replacing a shared process-policy value.

The distinction already has concrete consumers: [Hicasso's `capture-intents`](../../implementation/hicasso/test_kit/src/re_frame/hicasso/test.cljs) installs and removes an observer around a synchronous operation without changing the observed frame's configuration; [its server render watcher](../../implementation/hicasso/src/re_frame/hicasso/server.cljs) captures recovered, potentially frameless failures during one render. Moving those implementations to private registries preserves the framework's own privileges, but deliberately withdraws the same composable observation primitive from other programmers. That may be Mike's choice; it is not merely deleting another spelling.
DOSSIER ATTACHMENT (continued, piece 3/3, verbatim, contiguous with the previous piece):
**2. `local-raw` does not recover the substrate record.** [The event substrate](../../implementation/core/src/re_frame/event_emit.cljc) publishes `:time` and `:outcome`; [observability routing](../../implementation/core/src/re_frame/observability.cljc) constructs a different record with `:status`, effects and correlation, but no event timestamp. Non-event error attributes move under `:tags`. [Projection](../../implementation/core/src/re_frame/projection.cljc) still applies event-registration redaction before its frame-policy walker, even for `local-raw`. These can be sensible monitoring choices, but a profile changes projection, not the producer's record contract. Nor is the current event listener literally unprocessed raw data: its event vector is already wire-elided.

More importantly, the current event-centric sink route loses useful diagnosis **before projection**. [The error producer](../../implementation/core/src/re_frame/error_emit.cljc), `dispatch-on-error!`, builds `:source-coord` and category attribution such as `:failing-id`, `:reason`, `:flow-id` and `:op` into its corpus record, then calls `route-error!` without those attributes. Changing the egress profile cannot restore them. Losing which coeffect/interceptor failed is material to a productive production-monitoring API; fix or explicitly settle this before presenting sinks as a fully equivalent replacement.

**3. Dead-incarnation coverage cannot be implemented solely inside the routing fallback.** The same producer gates the entire sink call on `route-frame?`; `dispatch-error-record*` does likewise for post-dissociation teardown reports. When it is false, a new default inside `observability.cljc` is never reached. Moreover, the stale record's id may resolve successfully to a successor, so an unresolved-id test alone is insufficient. The [reincarnation regression](../../implementation/core/test/re_frame/capture_frame_reincarnation_sink_route_cljs_test.cljc) expressly preserves corpus delivery while suppressing successor-frame routing. An A1 implementation must carry this distinction through the producer seam: no authority to use a frame's policy, but permission to deliver through process policy, projecting with an explicitly absent owner. It must not re-resolve the stale id.

### Proportionate implementation and alternatives

For B, finish the already separated option-honesty, alias and teaching work; do not reopen the in-flight console change here. Update [the production how-to](../../docs/core/how-to/report-errors-in-production.md) and [API contract](../../spec/API.md) to state the real discriminator: **independent corpus observation versus policy-selected projected delivery**, including frameless and stale-incarnation coverage. Raw exception presence alone is indeed not the discriminator. Do not imply that default projection sanitizes arbitrary exception contents; its opaque-exception residual remains.

Separately, repair the dropped diagnostic attribution using an explicit set of structural fields and appropriate projected tree slots, not a blanket merge of arbitrary attributes into public summaries. Preserve query-vector identity and the existing category meanings. This improves the recommended monitoring path under every outcome.

If repeated configuration is the actual inconvenience, an application-owned shared policy value or frame-construction function is a smaller alternative; it solves repetition, not frameless delivery. If an actual host integration needs projected frameless delivery, C is a reasonable additive feature after rf2-kuky.5, but does not by itself justify later retirement. A is defensible only with an explicit ruling that independent public observation is being withdrawn, plus the attribution and producer-seam work above. Do not quietly turn a fallback into an additive global observer to recover parity: that is another routing model.

Focused acceptance for B: one sink and one temporary listener observe the same live failure with their documented shapes; listener capture still works with empty frame policy; removing it ends capture; and frameless/reincarnated failures retain the existing independent delivery without reaching a successor's sink. Attribution changes need a coeffect/interceptor example proving the projected record identifies the actual failing component. For A/C additionally test default inheritance versus `[]`, registered/missing/throwing sinks, and stale-owner fallback under a live unrelated ambient frame. These are meaningful cases, not a broad new observability framework.

The ethos here is a clear default plus an honest, small independent primitive. [Regularity and low hidden context](../../spec/Principles.md) favor that over reducing keyword count by adding ambient policy coupling.

## Problem

Spec 014's thesis is "single fx-id, single args map" (`spec/014-HTTPRequests.md:38`), and the tree honours it: every consumer ends at `[:rf.http/managed args-map]` → `re-frame.http.handlers/managed-handler`. Beside that door sits `re-frame.http` (`implementation/http/src/re_frame/http.cljc`, 129 lines): one private builder `build-managed-request-fx` (lines 44-51) and seven public fns `get` / `post` / `put` / `delete` / `patch` / `head` / `options` (lines 53-129), each `[url args]`, each returning `[:rf.http/managed (assoc args :request (assoc (:request args) :method <verb> :url url))]`. They hide nothing and save one map literal, and they cost a namespace, a `:refer-clojure :exclude [get]`, a manifest tier, three test files, a canonical-alias row, and the two-require trap the migration skill has to warn about (`skills/re-frame-migration/references/auto-cross-cutting.md:415`: `re-frame.http.managed` registers the fx, `re-frame.http` does not).

They also introduce a second place to say method/URL: the helper's `:method` / `:url` override anything under the caller's `:request` (`http.cljc:13-17`) — a precedence rule that exists only because one value is built through two surfaces. And they return an fx VECTOR, so the framework's own request-producing slots (resource / mutation `:request` producers, which consume managed-args MAPS) cannot use them at all.

## Target API

The data is the API. One way to issue a request:

```clojure
;; before (managed_http_counter/core.cljs:119)
:fx [(rf.http/get "api/inc.json" {:decode :json :reply-to [:http-counter/+1]})]

;; after
:fx [[:rf.http/managed {:request  {:method :get :url "api/inc.json"}
                        :decode   :json
                        :reply-to [:http-counter/+1]}]]
```

`:request` stays NESTED (codex, adopted): wire fields (`:method` `:url` `:headers` `:body` `:params`) and management fields (`:decode` `:retry` `:reply-to` `:request-id` `:timeout-ms`) are different concerns, and the resource/mutation producers depend on the nesting. App-level ergonomics are an app fn (the `rh/request` pattern) or a `:before` interceptor — never a framework verb family.

## Simpler elegant target

**The HTTP request API is one fx, one abort fx, one envelope, two registrar verbs, two canned fxs, and one test scope.**

```clojure

[:rf.http/managed {:request {:method :get :url "/api/items" …}
                   :decode  ItemList
                   :retry   {…}
                   :request-id :items/load
                   :reply-to [:items/loaded]}]          ; XOR :on-success / :on-failure

;; cancel (unchanged)

;; decorate — fn pair, frame-scoped (macro keeps source-coords; fx forms gone)

(rf/clear-http-interceptor :auth)                      ; (id) / (id {:frame f})

;; stub — home namespace only, one scope fn, one install pair, two canned fxs
(rf.http.test-support/with-request-stubs route-map thunk)   ; was with-managed-request-stubs*
(rf.http.test-support/install-request-stubs! route-map) / (uninstall-request-stubs!)
:rf.http/managed-canned-success / :rf.http/managed-canned-failure  ; via :fx-overrides
```

## Why this is better (ethos)

**Data before magic** (`spec/Principles.md:46`): "behaviour is expressible as data plus interpreter." `[:rf.http/managed {…}]` *is* that data. `(rf.http/get url args)` is a fn that returns the data with two keys pre-filled — it hides nothing, saves one map literal, and costs a namespace, a `:refer-clojure :exclude [get]`, a manifest tier, three test files, and the two-require trap the migration skill has to warn about (`skills/re-frame-migration/references/auto-cross-cutting.md:415`: "`re-frame.http` alone is verb helpers, it does **not** register the fx"). Clojure's answer to "typing `{:method :get}` is repetitive" is a `def`, not a library — and the flagship app already gave that answer with `rh/request`, which carries the policy a verb fn *cannot* (base URL, default decode, JSON encoding). The framework should teach that pattern, not compete with it.

**Regularity over cleverness** (`Principles.md:18`): "when a feature admits two shapes for the same job, designate one as canonical and the other as the documented alternative *with a stated use case*." The split/unified reply pair passes that bar (stated use case, measured demand). The verb helpers, the interceptor fxs, the stub macro, `:decode-schemas`, `:abort-signal` and `:accept` fail it: their alternative has no stated use case a consumer has exercised.

**The demand bar** (`Principles.md:124`): "a public surface ships only for a *named consumer*." Six verbs with zero consumers, two fxs whose only consumer is a harness that had to invent a DSL to use them, a metadata key nothing reads, an args key nothing sets: the bar has ruled retroactively. Pre-alpha means the tombstone is free now and expensive after the alpha tag.

**Named things over anonymous** (`Principles.md:24`) is the one principle the fx-form interceptor *appeals* to — "drive bootstrap through the dispatch surface." But an interceptor's payload is a fn; putting a fn inside an fx vector inside an event makes it *less* data-shaped, not more (the conformance corpus proves it by needing an interpreter). Registration belongs at boot with the other `reg-*` calls, which is where both real consumers put it.

**Honest costs.** (1) Deleting `re-frame.http` removes the only namespace-qualified reading cue ("`rf.http/get` reads as an HTTP GET") — the data form reads `:method :get` instead, which is the same word. (2) `:abort-signal` is the JS-interop escape hatch for an `AbortController` owned outside re-frame; deleting it means such a caller cancels via `:request-id` from a dispatch — one hop, cross-host, and already the documented preference (`014:726`). Park it with an un-park trigger (a named consumer holding a foreign controller) rather than keep it warm. (3) `:accept` gave a *typed* place for "2xx but domain-wrong"; without it the app decides in its success handler, which is where `realworld_http` already decides everything (`rh/failure->message`). Shrinking a closed set is a versioned change — do it now or never. (4) The `with-…` macro is idiomatic Clojure; the argument against it is purely demand (one file), and the fn form composes with `with-new-frame` and async wrappers where a macro body cannot.

## Codex cross-check (2026-09-05 10:37:13 AUSEST)

[`../codex/http-requests.md`](../codex/http-requests.md) concurs: the fx is the data, delete the seven verb fns (codex counted 3 literal `get` calls to this doc's 4). Three arguments from it are sharper than mine and are adopted: the helpers impose a precedence rule (helper method/url override anything in `:request`) that exists only because two surfaces build one value; the resource and mutation request producers consume managed-argument **maps**, not fx vectors, so the helpers cannot serve the framework's own more substantial request slots at all; and `:request` stays nested because wire fields (method, url, headers, body) and management fields (retry, decode, reply, correlation) are different concerns. Codex ranks this deletion below subscriptions and inspection and adds a fair caveat: if authoring trials show a real productivity loss, a deliberately justified convenience family beats insisting that more braces are elegant.

[`../codex/http-replies.md`](../codex/http-replies.md) first proposed `:reply-to` alone, then revised itself after checking this doc's login evidence at source: it now keeps both routing shapes and, like this doc, rejects mixing them. One teaching note survives from it: the counter example shares one event id between initiating a request and receiving its reply, so a `:cancelled` reply can fall into the initiation branch; a separate `:…/replied` receiver is the pattern to teach. ## Grok Thoughts

**Bother handling?** Yes. Spec 014's "single fx-id, single args map" is already true at the bottom; the accretion around it is not. Six of seven verb helpers have zero consumers. The flagship app never requires `re-frame.http` — it wrote `rh/request`, which is the pattern a verb fn *cannot* carry (base URL, default decode, JSON body). The interceptor fx pair's only consumer is a conformance DSL invented to describe a fn as data. `:abort-signal` and `:accept` are reserved slots nobody fills.

**Diagnosis.** Exact, including the three doc drifts (deleted 1-arity of `get`, a going-further sample that throws `:rf.error/http-no-reply-target`, "only `:request` is required" which has been false since reply targets became mandatory). The split-vs-unified re-measure (35 : 14, one login site that genuinely needs different event ids) is why the July ruling should stand. Codex's extra arguments — helper method/url override anything in `:request`; resource/mutation producers consume maps not fx vectors — make the verb-ns deletion stronger.

**Options.** Keep `get` as the one helper (4 sites) vs delete all seven. I would delete all seven: four sites is not a family, and a lone `get` re-introduces the two-require trap the migration skill has to warn about. Park vs delete for `:accept` / `:abort-signal`: park, with un-park triggers. Closed-set shrinks are versioned; pre-alpha is the moment, but "2xx but domain-wrong" is a real HTTP concept and a typed failure kind is cheaper to keep parked than to reconstruct.

**Recommendation.**

- The data *is* the API. Delete `re-frame.http`. Teach the app-local builder pattern from `realworld_http`.
- `:reply-to` XOR `:on-success`/`:on-failure`, rejection on key *presence* (nil still counts). `:reply-to nil` is the one fire-and-forget spelling. Do not reopen the split-sugar ruling.
- Delete both interceptor fx forms. Keep the macro/fn pair (source-coords). Registration is boot-time, which is where both real consumers put it.
- Delete the `[:http args]` API.md row (v1 residue, no such fx).
- Delete `:rf.http/decode-schemas` (9 duplicate writes, 0 tool readers). This *conflicts* with `schema-configuration-and-validation.md` item (d), which wants to keep the key and spread it to resources. Resolve: delete here; do not reuse an HTTP name on resources. `:decode` on the fx is the runtime truth.
- Park `:abort-signal` (un-park: a named consumer holding a foreign `AbortController`). Park `:accept` + `:rf.http/accept-failure` (un-park: a 2xx domain-failure that should not be a success-handler branch).
- Stub surface: keep canned fxs, `install-`/`uninstall-` (async/frame-creation), and the `*` fn (sync scope). Delete the macro twin and both facade re-exports (one test file).

**Implement.** One PR for verb-ns + XOR + interceptor fxs + `[:http]` row + `:decode-schemas` (all zero-or-four consumer). Parked keys can be the same PR if the closed-set change is accepted, else a follow-up. Four helper call sites become literal fx. Align the fx-form rule with `registration-spellings.md` so the two docs do not write different sentences. Fix the three doc drifts even if nothing is deleted.

## Codex Thoughts

**Verdict: worthwhile, but this dossier bundles straightforward API pruning with several distinct capability removals. Implement the small, well-supported simplifications first; do not approve the entire deletion list as one low-risk change.**

The seven verb constructors are genuine alternative spellings of managed-effect data. Keeping the raw args map also serves resource and mutation request producers, which need a map rather than a complete fx vector. Removing the helpers is reasonable pre-alpha, although it makes the shortest GET call longer. Correcting the phantom `[:http args]` and invalid examples is useful regardless of that decision.


Keep HTTP's two reply-routing shapes, but reject maps containing `:reply-to` alongside either branch key. The [sensitive-login example](../../../../examples/core/login/model.cljc) demonstrates why separate destinations can matter: success enters a credential-classified event, while failure enters the machine. This is pipeline selection, not merely spelling a `case` elsewhere.

Three proposed removals need stronger qualification:

- **`:accept` is not equivalent to checking the result in a success handler.** It classifies a decoded 2xx response before selecting the completion route. Moving the decision into an application receiver changes which event and pipeline receive it, and changes framework-level outcome classification. More importantly, the proposed `:after` replacement is **not presently equivalent**: [`dispatch-reply!`](../../../../implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/transport.cljc) selects the branch destination first; [`run-after-then-dispatch!`](../../../../implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/middleware.cljc) transforms the payload but passes the previously selected `:explicit-on` and `:kind` onward. Returning `{:status :error ...}` from `:after` can therefore send an error-shaped payload to the success destination. Either retain the small request-local normalization seam, or explicitly decide that domain outcomes belong entirely to application handlers and document the changed semantics. Do not redesign middleware merely to justify deleting it.
- **`:abort-signal` represents foreign lifecycle ownership.** A controller shared with non-re-frame operations is not equivalent to frame destruction or actor destruction. Bridging its signal to an application cancellation event is viable, but adds listener ownership and scheduling work for the programmer. Zero current callers supports parking that capability, not claiming it has already been replaced.
- **`:rf.http/decode-schemas` is a static declaration, whereas `:decode` belongs to a particular emitted request.** No tool reader is a good reason to stop carrying unused metadata, but a tool cannot generally reconstruct all possible decoder schemas from arbitrary handler code. Describe this as retiring an unconsumed declaration, not eliminating an identical copy.

Likewise, deleting the stub macro solely because its users are framework tests is weak: tests are legitimate consumers of a testing API. The important distinction is synchronous dynamic scope versus installation spanning asynchronous work, already explained in [`test_support.cljc`](../../../../implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/test_support.cljc). Keeping an idiomatic macro/function pair in its home namespace may be cheaper than renaming both and migrating callers.

Implement this as separate, proportionate changes: documentation corrections; reply-style exclusivity across real and canned paths; optional verb-helper retirement; then any explicitly accepted capability reductions. Verify split sensitive-login routing, explicit nil suppression, and request-map preservation. Elegant here means fewer authoring decisions without transferring hidden lifecycle or routing work to the application.

# HTTP request construction: verbs are data, not seven operations

Review date: 2026-09-05. Status: proposal only. Tracking bead: `rf2-snkw`.

## Finding

[re-frame.http](../../../../implementation/http/src/re_frame/http.cljc) exposes `get`, `post`, `put`, `delete`, `patch`, `head`, and `options`. Every function takes `[url args]` and delegates to `build-managed-request-fx`, which does essentially this:

```clojure
(let [request (assoc (clojure.core/get args :request {})
                     :method method :url url)]
  [:rf.http/managed (assoc args :request request)])
```

These are pure constructors of the already-public managed-effect vector. They do not send requests, choose a decoder, provide authentication, or establish an additional ownership contract. The other way to express exactly the same request is to write that effect data directly.

The helpers also introduce two places to express method/URL: their arguments override any values supplied inside `args :request`. The helper's precedence rule is sensible, but it is another rule needed only because the same value is being constructed through two surfaces.

## Known use cases and empirical evidence

| Use case | Repository evidence | Required capability |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A small successful GET with JSON decoding | [Managed HTTP counter](../../../../examples/core/managed_http_counter/core.cljs), `:http-counter/+1` | Method, URL, decode policy, and reply address. |
| A GET demonstrating failure classification | Same file, `:http-counter/fail` | The same request representation must preserve status-before-decoding behavior. The helper itself does not implement that behavior. |
| An inspector's live HTTP testbed | [Xray managed HTTP testbed](../../../../tools/xray/testbeds/managed_http/core.cljs), `::success` | A stable request ID and completion routing alongside the wire request. |
| Request construction with correlation and retry policy | [RealWorld HTTP articles](../../../../examples/real-apps/realworld_http/articles.cljs), `:articles/load` | Existing managed-effect maps carry request data and policy directly. |
| Shared URL/header/authentication policy and variable methods | [RealWorld shared HTTP](../../../../examples/real-apps/realworld_shared/http.cljs) | Compose ordinary request maps with application-specific knowledge; a generic verb helper does not remove that work. |
| Remote reads and writes owned by resources/mutations | [RealWorld resources](../../../../examples/real-apps/realworld_resources/resources.cljs), [mutations](../../../../examples/real-apps/realworld_resources/mutations.cljs) | Request producers return managed-HTTP argument maps; the runtime supplies addressing/ownership. A helper returning an effect vector is not the value these slots consume. |

| Controlled effects in stories and demo backends | [Story login events](../../../../tools/story/testbeds/login_form/events.cljs), [RealWorld demo backend](../../../../examples/real-apps/realworld_shared/demo_backend.cljs) | Inspect or replace the effect data without a constructor-specific protocol. |
| The rest of the HTTP verbs, request bodies, and caller-supplied request options | Helper implementations and [helper integration tests](../../../../implementation/http/test/re_frame/http_helpers_integration_test.clj) | Preserve the transport's supported methods and request fields, including uncommon methods; removing constructors is not removing HTTP capabilities. |

In the qualified helper-call search of authored examples/tools Clojure-family source, I found three literal GET calls: two in the counter and one in Xray. I found no literal calls there to the other six verb helpers. This is a bounded repository observation, not a claim that external applications cannot use them. The larger examples already demonstrate the data representation and domain-specific request composition.

Follow-on verification from [Fable's wider census](../fable/http-request-surface.md) adds a fourth GET site in [the separate HTTP-toggle testbed](../../../../testbeds/http_toggle/core.cljs). This expands the search boundary to `/testbeds`; it does not contradict the examples/tools count. Its request uses the same existing helper and `:reply-to`. The recommendation is unchanged.

## Proposed smaller API

Use the existing managed-effect representation as the canonical authoring surface. Remove the seven verb constructors from the supported public API; do not replace them with seven macros or a second builder family.

```clojure
;; Existing supported representation; proposed as the sole library-level form.
{:fx [[:rf.http/managed
       {:request {:method :get :url "/api/articles"}
        :decode :json
        :reply-to [:articles/replied]}]]}
```

For dynamic requests, `:method` simply contains the chosen keyword. Ordinary functions can return request or managed-argument maps, and event handlers can put those values into the effect vector. An application can still define a meaningful function such as `save-article-request`; trusting the programmer means not forbidding useful local abstractions.

Keep `:request` nested. Wire fields such as URL, headers, body and method differ from management fields such as retry, decoding, reply routing and correlation. Flattening them would mix concerns and complicate resource/mutation composition. Keep transport installation and the managed HTTP engine; this proposal removes constructors, not the effect interpreter or its lifecycle.

The [reply-addressing finding](http-replies.md) is independent. Constructor removal works even if split success/failure routing remains supported.

## Counterargument and migration

`(http/get url opts)` is genuinely shorter than a literal effect vector containing a request map. The counter example even explains that advantage in its comments. Short, familiar authoring has value; function-count reduction alone is not sufficient justification.

My recommendation favors the data form because it is already necessary for the more substantial request-producing surfaces, composes directly with ordinary map operations, and is used by the larger examples. The convenience family adds almost no domain knowledge. This is lower-priority than the subscription and inspection findings: if authoring trials show a material productivity loss, keeping a deliberately justified convenience family is better than insisting that more braces are elegant by definition.

Migration is mechanical: replace each helper call with an equivalent effect vector, merging its existing nested request map while preserving the helper's method/URL override precedence. Computed helper values or higher-order references need corresponding function rewrites rather than textual substitution. Do not drop headers/body or accidentally relocate decode/retry options into `:request`.

The resource/mutation request producers should remain maps, not acquire an effect-vector wrapping/unwrapping convention. Demo backends and stubs should continue receiving the same managed arguments. No compatibility option or new constructor registry is needed.

## Why this is more elegant

HTTP method is a dimension of a request value, not seven distinct framework capabilities. In Clojure, the useful abstraction is the request data plus the interpreter that performs it. Data remains inspectable, composable, serializable where its contents allow, and easy for a tool or AI to transform.

This follows [Vision's data-oriented computational model](../../../../spec/000-Vision.md) without turning “data over APIs” into a ban on functions. Keep functions where they express application intent; avoid library wrappers whose entire meaning is one `assoc` around an already-supported value.

## Focused acceptance evidence

Compare old helper output with replacement data for every verb, preserving nested fields and override precedence. Migrate the three observed helper calls and run their focused integration coverage. Confirm that resource request maps, SSR and story stubs require no new representation. No transport redesign or broad HTTP policy review is necessary for this subtraction.

Include the separately verified HTTP-toggle call in that migration as well. Fable proposes additional HTTP option, interceptor-effect, and stub deletions; those are separate decisions, not prerequisites for removing the verb constructors.

# HTTP replies: two useful routing shapes, no mixed precedence

Review date: 2026-09-05. Status: proposal only. Tracking bead: `rf2-snkw`.

Revised after considering [Fable's HTTP review](../fable/http-request-surface.md) and checking its login example against source. This supersedes my initial recommendation to remove split success/failure addressing. The useful reduction is narrower: retain the two meaningful routing shapes, remove their mixture.

## Finding

Managed HTTP accepts three addressing fields: `:reply-to`, `:on-success`, and `:on-failure`. Yet all deliver the same canonical reply map, with `:status :ok`, `:error`, or `:cancelled` and the corresponding value/error and work metadata. [HTTP reply construction](../../../../implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/reply.cljc) explicitly documents that there is no separate public success/failure payload dialect.

[Validation and normalization](../../../../implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/handlers.cljc) require at least one addressing key. A branch-specific key overrides `:reply-to`; explicit nil differs from absence. [Reply event encoding](../../../../implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/encoding.cljc), at `build-reply-event`, appends the canonical envelope to a vector target, suppresses explicitly nil destinations, and handles missing branches. This introduces precedence and missing-versus-nil rules around what is otherwise one result protocol.

This is real overlap, but not total semantic equivalence: branch-specific destinations can choose different registered event pipelines, and suppressing a branch can avoid dispatch altogether. Any simplification must admit those costs.

## Known use cases and empirical evidence

| Use case | Repository evidence | Implication |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One receiver handles success and failure | [Managed HTTP counter](../../../../examples/core/managed_http_counter/core.cljs), `:http-counter/+1` and `:http-counter/fail` | Existing `:reply-to` already supplies the common vocabulary. The handlers inspect `:status`. |
| Both branch fields name the same receiver | [Xray HTTP testbed](../../../../tools/xray/testbeds/managed_http/core.cljs), `::success` | `:on-success [::reply]` plus `:on-failure [::reply]` is a direct duplicate of `:reply-to [::reply]`. |
| Different success and failure handlers | [RealWorld HTTP articles](../../../../examples/real-apps/realworld_http/articles.cljs), `:articles/load`, `:articles/loaded`, `:articles/load-failed` | Combining routing requires inspecting the actual handler logic and metadata, not just renaming fields. |
| Different reply destinations protect different data and event shapes | [Shared login model](../../../../examples/core/login/model.cljc), `:auth.login/submit-form` and `:auth.login/succeeded` | Success goes to a handler whose map payload classifies the token as sensitive; failure goes directly to the login machine. These are genuinely different pipelines. |
| Only one outcome is interesting | Xray testbed's synthetic 4xx/5xx effects; [SSR articles load](../../../../examples/capabilities/ssr/ssr/core.cljc) uses only `:on-success` | A unified receiver may deliberately return no effects for an irrelevant outcome, but that is still a delivered event. |
| Capture application context in the reply address | RealWorld HTTP article loading; [resource article editor](../../../../examples/real-apps/realworld_resources/article_editor.cljs) | Preserve the event-vector prefix and append the full reply once; do not move correlation into hidden state. |
| A shared completion idiom across managed features | [Resource settings](../../../../examples/real-apps/realworld_resources/settings.cljs) and article editor | Resources/mutations already demonstrate `:reply-to`-style completion handlers; HTTP need not teach another primary idiom. |
| HTTP owned by a state machine | [HTTP machine wrapper](../../../../implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/machine_wrapper.cljc), `make-machine-spec` | It currently selects internal `:rf.http/succeeded` / `:rf.http/failed` signals. The machine must still transition correctly on outcome. |

| Explicit fire-and-forget | Validation/encoding contracts: `:reply-to nil` | Keep a deliberate no-destination form. Do not restore implicit replies to the originating event. |
| Cancellation, stale suppression, and failure diagnostics | HTTP reply/encoding/transport paths | `:cancelled` is an outcome, not missing data; addressing changes must not alter ownership, abort, or stale-work rules. |
| Deterministic canned completions | [HTTP test support](../../../../implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/test_support.cljc), `emit-canned-success!` / `emit-canned-failure!` | Tests and live transport must share destination/envelope semantics without fabricating production work identity. |

Some rows are supported-contract cases rather than observed application preferences. In particular, fire-and-forget and the full cancellation contract should not be presented as frequent app call patterns on this evidence.

## What changed my recommendation

The login example routes success to `[:auth.login/succeeded]`, whose registration declares `:sensitive [[:value :token]]`; the appended reply is its addressable map payload. Failure goes to `[:auth.login/flow [:auth.login/failure]]`. The successful handler stores the token and sends a credential-free success signal to the machine. This is source-backed evidence for the pipeline distinction I had previously treated mainly as a migration caveat.

A single receiver could reproduce this with more application routing code. That does not make the library more ergonomic. Fewer keys would move complexity into a real application, adding a forwarding event or changing its classified handler boundary. Under the user's low-friction posture, retain the split.

## Proposed smaller API

Allow exactly one addressing style per request:

```clojure
;; One receiver handles the complete result.
{:request {:method :get :url "/api/articles"}
 :reply-to [:articles/replied]}

;; Different outcomes have different receivers.
{:request {:method :post :url "/api/login" :body credentials}
 :on-success [:auth.login/succeeded]
 :on-failure [:auth.login/flow [:auth.login/failure]]}

;; Deliberately no receiver.
{:request {:method :post :url "/api/telemetry"}
 :reply-to nil}
```

The snippets show addressing, not the complete login application's sensitive-request configuration. Keep the existing canonical envelope, branch-only routing, explicit nil, cancellation and failure diagnostics. The proposed change is to reject a map containing `:reply-to` together with either branch key, instead of applying per-branch override precedence. Key presence matters even when its value is nil.

Fable's census found no mixed-style application consumers. I verified the cited actual split, unified, same-target and nil-target examples; I am not independently certifying every count in its broader census.

Use `:reply-to` when both outcomes name the same handler, as in Xray. Use `:reply-to nil` instead of writing both branch keys as nil, as in the login cancellation demonstration. Keep distinct destinations in login, RealWorld articles and the HTTP machine. No compatibility switch, new routing map, or blanket handler rewrite is needed.

## Why this is more elegant

The distinction now has a simple explanation: one receiver for a result, or different receivers for different outcomes. Mixing both is a third interpretation with no demonstrated need.

This applies [regularity and named things](../../../../spec/Principles.md) to the programmer's task rather than just the manifest. The result remains data, destinations remain ordinary named events, and the programmer keeps useful control over their event pipelines. Elegance is removing an unnecessary rule, not requiring an adapter event to save two option names.

## Focused acceptance evidence

Reject mixed styles; normalize the same-target and all-nil examples; preserve login's sensitive success handler, direct machine failure, and existing one-branch behavior. Confirm live and canned replies agree. The old success/failure handler timing and cancellation/ownership rules should otherwise remain unchanged.

# Reply addressing — five spellings for "where does the completion land"

**Status:** high (cross-surface vocabulary divergence; wave 2, 2026-07-10 14:30 AUSEST, Fable-authored)
**Surfaces:** `:rf/reply-to` (canonical target), HTTP `:on-success` / `:on-failure`, the co-located `:rf/reply` default, resources/mutations bare `:reply-to`, machine `:on-done` / `:on-error`

---

## The problem

The reply **envelope** is uniform (Managed-Effects property 9 — one `:status`-keyed map across every
async family; the l7s7b7 migration just unified its field keys too). The **addressing** is not. One
concept — *which event receives the completion* — has five public spellings:

| Spelling | Surface | What it lowers to |
|---|---|---|
| `:rf/reply-to` | the canonical descriptor/target key | — (it IS the internal form) |
| `:on-success` / `:on-failure` | HTTP args map | `:rf/reply-to` (pure routing sugar; both get the identical envelope) |
| *(omit everything)* → co-located `:rf/reply` | HTTP default | reply routes back to the **requesting event id**, merged under `:rf/reply`; handler branches on presence |
| `:reply-to` (bare) | resources `ensure`/`refetch`, mutations `execute` | `:rf/reply-to` |
| `:on-done` / `:on-error` | machine spawn/nodes | machine-native **transitions** (listed as reply sugar in Managed-Effects, but they are statechart grammar, not call-site addressing) |

Worse than the count: the *same key* is spelled three ways across surfaces (`:rf/reply-to` canonical,
bare `:reply-to` in resources, a key-pair in HTTP), and HTTP does **not** accept the canonical key at
all (`docs/async/continuations-are-data.md:147`).

---

## Empirical use cases

### 1. HTTP fetch landing in success/failure events — **dominant**

42 call-sites across 18 example files; every fetch in `realworld_http`, all three `login` ports,
`nine_states`, `boot`, the machine walkthrough.

```clojure
:on-success [:comments/loaded]  :on-failure [:comments/load-failed]
```

### 2. Mutation / read completion continuation (resources)

~6 call-sites, all in `realworld_resources` (`settings.cljs:86`, `article_editor.cljs:364,413`,
`views.cljs:156,186`, ensure at `article_editor.cljs:278`) — spelled **bare `:reply-to`**.

### 3. Zero-config co-located default

One dedicated showcase (`managed_http_counter`, ~13 `:rf/reply` reads) plus exactly **one** handler in
`realworld_http/comments.cljs:99`, kept deliberately as a contrast demo ("one handler, two roles").

### 4. Machine child completion

`:on-done` / `:on-error` — zero uses in `examples/`; one Xray testbed. Machine examples that do HTTP
use `:on-success`/`:on-failure`, not `:on-done`.

### 5. Direct `:rf/reply-to` authoring

**Zero** app or tool call-sites anywhere. It exists in spec, EP-0011, impl, and conformance probes
only. The canonical public key is, empirically, not a public key.

### 6. Same intent, mixed spellings in one codebase

`realworld_resources` uses `:reply-to` for CRUD **and** `:on-success`/`:on-failure` for its auth HTTP
(`auth.cljs:259-279`) — both addressing styles in one app. `realworld_http/comments.cljs` uses
co-located addressing for one fetch and explicit sugar for the rest of the same file.

---

## Simpler elegant target

### One authoring key, one normalization, per-surface sugar that earns its place

1. **Every async managed effect accepts bare `:reply-to`** in its args map — resources already do; HTTP
   and any future surface gain it. It normalizes to the internal `:rf/reply-to` descriptor — the
   established authoring-key → owner-qualified-slot pattern (`:select-ns` → `:rf.image/*`,
   `:initial-events` → `:rf.frame/initial-events`). `:rf/reply-to` stops being presented as an
   app-facing spelling at all: it is the normalized internal name and the conformance surface.
2. **HTTP keeps `:on-success` / `:on-failure`** — 42 sites say this sugar earns its place (status-split
   routing is the ergonomic winner for fetches). It remains *pure* sugar over the same lowering.
3. **Retire the co-located `:rf/reply` default.** Empirical demand: one showcase + one handler. In
   exchange for that, every HTTP request silently owns a second job for its requesting handler
   ("branch on `:rf/reply` presence") — implicit dual-role handlers are exactly the ambient magic the
   framework rejects elsewhere. Omitting a target becomes **fail-loud** ("no reply target — add
   `:on-success`/`:on-failure` or `:reply-to`"). Pre-alpha, tombstone-free; the showcase demo rewrites
   to explicit sugar.
4. **Stop calling machine `:on-done`/`:on-error` reply sugar.** They are statechart transitions
   (XState parity surface), not call-site addressing; Managed-Effects should list them as the machine
   family's *native completion grammar* that lowers onto the envelope internally. No API change — a
   framing fix that removes a whole row from the addressing table.

Result: the addressing story is one sentence — **"say `:reply-to`; on HTTP you may say
`:on-success`/`:on-failure` instead"** — and the table above collapses from five rows to two.

---

## Why this is better (ethos)

**re-frame2:** one name per fact is the corpus's deepest naming law, and it currently fails at the
call-site layer of its flagship async story: the same fact (reply target) is spelled differently per
surface, and the canonical spelling has zero consumers. Uniform envelope + uniform addressing is what
makes "learn one managed effect, know them all" true rather than aspirational.

**Fail-loud over silent default:** the co-located default routes replies *somewhere* when the author
said nothing — the one place in the async story where omission produces behaviour instead of an error.
The framework's own no-silent-swallow rule points the other way.

**Clojure:** bare keys in a closed args map are the local grammar (regime 1); the owner-qualified twin
belongs to the internal normalized form (regime 2). The current split has the regimes backwards on two
surfaces.

**Masterpiece:** the reply envelope was unified by design; the addressing grew by per-surface accretion.
Finish the thought.

---

## Non-goals

- Do not touch the envelope shape or field keys (just ruled and migrated — l7s7b7).
- Do not remove `:on-success` / `:on-failure` (dominant, ergonomic, pure sugar).
- Do not rebuild machine completion as call-site reply addressing (`:on-done` is statechart grammar;
  parity-protected).
- Do not add a `:reply-to` to non-async effects (the envelope is async-only — property 9).

## Grok Thoughts

**Bother handling?** Yes, and the work landed: `:reply-to` unified, co-located `:rf/reply` default retired, omitting all targets throws. Wave 3 re-measured the split (35 `:on-*` : 14 `:reply-to`) and found one login site that genuinely needs different event ids with different arities. That is the evidence that should have been in this doc's "keep the sugar" argument; it arrived later and correctly stopped Codex from collapsing to a single receiver.

**Diagnosis, in hindsight.** The five-row table mixed two jobs: call-site addressing (`:reply-to` / `:on-*` / co-located default) and machine *statechart* completion (`:on-done` / `:on-error`). Calling the latter "reply sugar" was the framing error this doc already caught. The co-located default was the real silent-swallow: omission produced behaviour. Retiring it was right.

**What is left.** The unused three-key precedence (`:reply-to` *plus* `:on-*` as per-branch override, zero consumers). Wave 3 HTTP proposes XOR on key presence, with `:reply-to nil` as the one fire-and-forget spelling. Do that in the HTTP bead; do not reopen this ruling. Teach a separate `:…/replied` receiver — the counter example sharing one event id between initiate and reply is how a `:cancelled` reply falls into the initiation branch.

**Do not.** Rebuild machine completion as call-site addressing. That is `machine-child-lifecycle-and-addressing.md`'s join unification, a different fact. Do not touch the envelope.

## Codex Thoughts

**Verdict: the central recommendation was good and has substantially landed. Treat this July dossier as historical rationale, not a fresh five-spelling defect.**

The current [`validate-reply-target!` and `normalise-args`](../../../../implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/handlers.cljc) already accept bare `:reply-to`, retain split `:on-success`/`:on-failure`, and reject omission of every reply target before starting the request. The implicit co-located `:rf/reply` fallback is retired. Consequently, the original use counts and “HTTP gains it” instructions no longer describe implementation work outstanding.

The remaining useful simplification is the unused **mixed-style precedence rule**. Require either `:reply-to` or branch addressing, never both. Check key presence, not truthiness: `{:reply-to nil :on-success [:done]}` still mixes two grammars. Continue allowing either branch key alone and preserve explicit nil suppression; the choice is between routing styles, not a requirement to write both branches.

The diagnosis should also distinguish common envelopes from interchangeable destinations. The [login model](../../../../examples/core/login/model.cljc) sends success to a handler whose map payload is classified for credential redaction and failure directly to a machine event. A unified receiver can represent the business logic, but replacing these destinations is not a mechanical normalization: interceptors, coeffects, schemas, trace identity, payload shape, and possibly an additional dispatch change. The split form earns its place through this concrete use case, not merely through its call count.

Viable targets are therefore:

- Keep the existing two styles, removing only mixed-style precedence — recommended.
- Keep one receiver everywhere and require application-level status branching — superficially smaller, but not a justified improvement for existing distinct pipelines.
- Introduce a status-to-event map — another routing mini-language with little benefit over the familiar branch keys.

Implement the recommended target in the real request validator and corresponding canned/stub normalization. Preserve omitted-versus-explicit-nil behavior and check that a rejected mixed map issues no request. Use `:reply-to nil` in teaching examples for intentional silence, without adding a separate fire-and-forget operation. An example that shares an event id between initiation and completion should explicitly distinguish cancelled replies from initiation; otherwise a cancellation can accidentally look like a request to start again.

Finally, the original decision to separate machine grammar from HTTP addressing remains correct. [`finalize.cljc`](../../../../implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/lifecycle_fx/finalize.cljc) still treats single-child `:on-done` as a parent-data fold and `:on-error` as a transition. Their names should not be forced into the HTTP args-map grammar. The separate terminal-completion proposal concerns reusable children across `:spawn` and `:spawn-all`, not one universal callback API.

## The decision in one sentence

Two examples carry a second host page, `stories.index.html`, that no documented route serves and that differs from `index.html` only in `<title>`/meta and a head comment: delete both pages and let `index.html` be the documented host for both builds (A), teach the shared runner to prefer `<prefix>.index.html` for a `*-host` build so the showcase gets its own tab title (B), or leave both pages in place (C).

**Letters.** The two source beads lettered this oppositely to each other (rf2-fn0kx.10 finding 1: A = keep and teach the runner, B = retire; rf2-fn0kx.5 finding 3: A = delete, B = teach the runner). Rule by THIS dossier's letters: **A = retire, B = teach the runner, C = keep as they are.**

```
npm run dev:example -- examples/login-with-stories
...
serve-example: examples/login-with-stories is live at http://127.0.0.1:8050/
```

(`serve-example.cjs:550` prints that line; 8050 is the default band.) The browser tab reads **"re-frame2 example: login (state-machine demo)"** (`login/index.html:5`) — the plain example's title, because the staged page IS `index.html`: PR #10182's worker fetched `/` and found it byte-identical to the source `index.html` (1781 bytes, 2 host attributes) and different from `stories.index.html`. Append `#/stories` and the Story shell mounts on the same page; Ctrl+Shift+C opens Xray inline in the aside on either surface. Nothing fails. The showcase's own title, **"re-frame2 example: login (with Stories + Xray)"** (`login/stories.index.html:5`), and its OG card are never shown. nine_states is the same story with "nine states" in place of "login".

Under the other documented route, `npx shadow-cljs watch :examples/login-with-stories` then `http://localhost:8041/`: `index.html` again, by root order (`shadow-cljs.edn:637-638`), and unstyled because `_shared/` is not staged there (PR #10165 corrected the README to say so). `http://localhost:8041/stories.index.html` would show the other title — reasoned from the `:roots`, not run.

**Under A (retire):** the reader's experience is byte-for-byte what it is today. `git ls-files examples/core/login` loses one entry; the README file list at `login/README.md:71-81` becomes

```
  stories.cljs         — Story showcase: variants covering every reachable

  stories_host.cljs    — Story-showcase entry point (live-app <-> shell hash router).
```

and `examples/README.md:165` says "a `stories.cljs` + `stories_host.cljs` pair". The only thing lost is a tab title / OG card that has never been displayed by any documented route. (.-title js/document) "re-frame2 example: login (with Stories + Xray)")` — recovers it with no second page; my suggestion, not part of the ruling, and I would not bother.)

**Under B (teach the runner):** `examples-staging.cjs:367` becomes roughly

```js
const last = ns.replace(/^.*\./, '');                 // "stories-host"
const prefix = last.endsWith('-host') ? last.slice(0, -5) : null;
const showcase = prefix && path.join(srcDir, `${prefix}.index.html`);
const htmlSrc = showcase && io.existsSync(showcase) ? showcase : path.join(srcDir, 'index.html');
```

and `dev:example -- examples/login-with-stories` stages `stories.index.html`, so the tab reads "login (with Stories + Xray)" while `examples/login` keeps the plain title. ## Options

### A. Retire both `stories.index.html` pages; `index.html` is the host for both builds (rf2-fn0kx.10's "B", rf2-fn0kx.5's "A", the bead's own recommendation, the earlier draft's and the Codex agent's)
- What changes: `git rm` the two pages. `login/README.md`: drop `:77-81`, "The 3 `stories*` files" at `:84` becomes "two". `nine_states/README.md`: drop `:169-173`, `:177` likewise. `examples/README.md:165`: "trio" becomes "pair", drop the filename. `examples/_shared/README.md:55`: drop "`index.html` and `stories.index.html` alike" (rf2-3p85d is closed, so the file is free). `check-examples-assets.cjs:324-333`: rewrite the comment to say the `<prefix>.index.html` shape is kept prospectively and no such page exists under `examples/` today (`isExampleHostPage` at `:357-359` stays — it costs nothing and its unit test at `:202-209` still holds). `check-examples-assets.test.cjs:211-223`: delete the LIVE pin (the TEETH tests at `:1549-1595` keep the shape's teeth on synthetic paths). Both `index.html` head comments already say the truth and need no edit.
- Consequences: programmer sees no change; AI reads a README that matches the tree; the asset gate scans 31 pages (floor 10); Story and Xray unaffected; no spec sentence moves (the Story spec never names these pages; `spec/` has 0 references outside `findings/`).
- Cost: **half a worker-morning.** 2 deletions + 6 edits (4 READMEs, 1 script comment, 1 test); 0 hot-zone files; 0 `.cljs`/`.edn`; no shadow-cljs lane needed (CI's `examples_compile` arms on `examples/*` anyway).
- Risk: someone who typed `/stories.index.html` under a bare watch loses it — no README or launcher names that URL, so the population is whoever wrote the pages.

### B. Keep the pages and teach `listStandaloneExamples` to prefer `<prefix>.index.html` for a `*-host` init-fn (rf2-fn0kx.10's "A", rf2-fn0kx.5's "B")
- What changes: the four-line rule above at `examples-staging.cjs:367`; one assertion each for both showcase builds in `_examples-staging.test.cjs:324-329`; rewrite both `stories.index.html` head comments (`login:22-30`, `nine_states:16-20`), both `index.html` head comments (`login:22-25`, `nine_states:22-26`), both README file-list entries (`:77-81`, `:169-173`) and both README run sentences (`login:100`, `nine_states:205-208`). Decide separately what to say about the watch route, which keeps serving `index.html` at `/` (`shadow-cljs.edn:634-639` is a hot-zone file, and no edit there can change which filename answers `/`).
- Consequences: the showcase gets its own tab title and OG card on the `dev:example` route only; the runner acquires a naming convention that the tree's one other consumed `<prefix>.index.html` does not use (`story-build.cjs:82-100` selects by explicit constant); two pages per example stay in sync by hand forever, which is the mechanism that produced #10174's wrong-page fix.
- Cost: **one worker-morning.** 1 shared script + 1 test + 4 HTML + 3 READMEs; hot-zone only if the watch route is touched.
- Risk: the reviewer's own "latent trap" (rf2-fn0kx.10 finding 1) inverts rather than closes — an edit to `index.html` is now the one the showcase's `dev:example` route silently ignores, while the watch route still shows it.

### C. Keep both pages exactly as they are
- What changes: nothing in the tree — but the six "open call / until settled" passages become false once ruled, so an honest C edits four comments and two README entries to say the pages are deliberate, and updates nothing else.
- Consequences: the LIVE pin, the sync duty, the "trio" wording and the unserved title all persist; the only benefit over A is the `/stories.index.html` URL under a bare watch.
- Cost: 0 if the stale "open call" prose is tolerated; otherwise 6 comment/README edits, most of A's cost for none of its subtraction.
- Risk: the next person to touch either page repeats #10174.

## Recommendation
(DOSSIER continued, part 2 of 2)

**A.** Under the stance this is the plainest case in the wave: a file that no documented route has ever served, kept for a tab title on `127.0.0.1`, is minutiae, and the project has already lost a worker cycle to it (the #10174 fix landing on the unserved page, then rf2-7w1vm to land it again). B is gold plating in the exact sense the stance names — a naming convention added to a shared runner, plus a permanent two-page sync duty, to display an OG card that no crawler will fetch from localhost — and it cannot even make the two documented routes agree. C carries B's sync duty with none of its benefit. "Trust the programmer" cuts the same way: the READMEs already tell the reader the showcase is "the same page plus `#/stories`", and that sentence is true today; A makes the tree match it.

What would change my mind: a decision to publish the two showcases as static, user-facing pages (the `013-Static-Build.md` shape), where a distinct title and OG card are seen by real readers. Even then the mechanism would be the static build's explicit `STORY_BUILD_INDEX_HTML`-style selection, not a runner naming rule — so B's script change would still not be the thing to build.

title: False: Xray embedding contract says the shell shares the host's React tree
description: Merged-PR audit #9711, confirmed at ec73b0774bb38db80c421c8265bf6db6405e4d46. tools/xray/spec/008-Embedding-Contract.md:325 says Xray's shell mounts inside the host's React tree and uses that premise to explain state isolation. That is false: Story's panel-host-component appends a container and calls a mount function; panels/render-panel! and panels/mount-shell! create an independent root through the installed adapter, while mount/open!, open-overlay! and popout! use Xray's own Fresco client roots. DOM containment does not make a separate React root inherit the host's React context. Xray supplies its own frame context explicitly. The mismatch predates the root swap, so describe it as a correction of the embedding contract, not newly introduced runtime behavior. The PR correctly identified it, but its required correction was recorded only in rf2-k97c.6/rf2-k97c.7 implementation notes; this issue makes that concrete defect separately trackable. Correct the State isolation explanation to distinguish DOM placement, React-root ownership and explicit frame selection; preserve the documented own-frame versus target-frame semantics. No production change is requested.

It accurately explains the independent mount root and explicit Xray frame-provider, consistent with panels/render-panel!, panels/mount-shell! and the owned shell mount verbs. WHAT WAS FALSE. 008's "## State isolation (Option-C frame-provider)" opened:
"Xray's shell mounts **inside the host's React tree** so embedding is zero-config"
and then built the whole state-isolation explanation on that premise.

WHAT REPLACED IT. A three-way split, because the three things the old sentence
collapsed are what a reader actually needs kept apart:
  * DOM PLACEMENT — where the shell's node sits in the host's document. The host
    decides, via the mount-point / layout host.
  * REACT-ROOT OWNERSHIP — which root renders the shell's tree. NEVER the host's.
    open! / open-overlay! / popout! paint through a re-frame.fresco client root Xray
    owns; panels/mount-shell! and the mount-<panel>! facades call
    rf.substrate.adapter/render, which creates its OWN root at the mount-point.
    Either way it is a separate root.
  * FRAME SELECTION — which frame descendant reads and dispatches resolve to. Xray,
    explicitly.

AND THE MECHANISM, which is the part that makes the correction stick: DOM containment
is not React containment. React context does not cross a root boundary, so a host's
frame-provider is NOT in scope inside the embed however deeply the node is nested,
and there is no host frame for the shell to fall through TO. That is a property of
React rather than of Xray, which is why reading the mount code alone never settles
it. Cited on the page to the row that MEASURES it —
w5-the-embed-door-mounts-and-never-touches-the-host-frames-ring in
shell_fresco_boundary_dom_cljs_test — which mounts the embed inside a host Reagent
root under [rf/frame-provider {:frame app}], drives a real click, and asserts the
host frame's epoch ring is unchanged in COUNT and CONTENTS, beside a control showing
the same ring does move for a genuine application event.

only here: THE MISMATCH PREDATES THE ROOT SWAP. render-panel!'s adapter/render made
its own root as far back as rf2-tijr, so the sentence was already misleading before
rf2-k97c.3 and the swap merely made it conspicuous. It is written as a correction of
the embedding contract, NOT as behaviour the swap introduced.

untouched — that subsection is unchanged.

ALSO PRESERVED, and worth naming because it would have been easy to lose: the
correction does NOT weaken the isolation story, it strengthens it. Isolation no
longer rests on the frame-provider wrapper alone. The wrapper makes the shell's reads
and dispatches land in a NAMED frame; the root boundary makes the host's frame

## Problem

At tip every tool-side projection of a bare value reaches the framework's classification WALKER rather than the boundary door: pair-MCP renders `(re-frame.core/elide-wire-value v opts)` into eval strings from nine builders, story-mcp calls `rf/elide-wire-value` for app-db (while ALREADY calling `rf/project-egress` with a profile for derived trees), Xray's clipboard/console egress hand-rolls the off-box floor onto the walker, the pair preload calls the walker twice, and Story calls the HOME namespace `re-frame.elision/elide-wire-value` for assertion and error records. The walker does not read `:rf.egress/profile` (0 occurrences in `implementation/core/src/re_frame/elision.cljc`), so the two MCP servers render policy BOOLEANS for it — which is the only reason `tools/mcp-base` carries a pure-data MIRROR of the framework's profile table (`tools/mcp-base/src/re_frame/mcp_base/egress.cljc:56-106`, pinned byte-equal to `implementation/core/src/re_frame/projection.cljc:124-163` by the `mcp-conformance-wire-vocab` gate). Under ruling A the servers name a PROFILE and the app-side door resolves it. `rf/project-egress` on a kindless value IS the walker (`projection.cljc:482-497`) plus profile resolution (`:191-221`), so every migration below is output-identical when the chosen profile resolves to the floor the caller hand-rolls today.

This stage is FIRST because stage 2 deletes the facade walker export: deleting first would leave Xray's compiled `rf/elide-wire-value` call (`tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/egress.cljs:87`) failing to compile and pair-MCP's rendered forms failing at eval time. Every tool-side projection call is `(rf/project-egress v-or-record opts)` with a profile from the closed enum (`projection.cljc:90-97`); no tool renders or passes `:rf.size/*` booleans as a FLOOR.
